verdicts.why: A's thirteen pills are the fields this reader would file under (computational neuroscience, consciousness, Buddhism, AI, AI safety, writing, philosophy of science) with sound membership and useful intersections, and they reach the whole shelf. B is bare keywords ('training', 'agent', 'prediction') that lump meditation with model training and Popper with dopamine, hold three or four articles each, and leave Buddhism, writing, economics and most of the shelf unreachable.

A's six labels are the right high-level concepts and cover nearly the whole shelf, but membership is loose: 'Philosophy of science' swallows economics, history of science and Ray Dalio, 'Artificial intelligence' holds central banks, and learning-science pieces sit under computational neuroscience. It still beats B easily, whose keyword pills are arbitrary, tiny and leave most of the shelf with no pill at all.

Both use real concepts, but B splits the shelf into thirteen clean topics (economics, history of science, learning and memory, productivity, AI safety, meditation each get their own pill) with accurate membership and useful pairings like Buddhism + Meditation or AI + Economics. A's six buckets are too coarse and misfiled: 28 articles under 'Philosophy of science' including housing costs and auctions, and central banks under AI.
